title: Count the work in a search
summary: Compare a scan with interval halving while separating theoretical cost from timing.
objectives: Specify a search contract, input size, representation, and counted operation.
Trace successful, unsuccessful, and empty searches without confusing examinations with elapsed time.
Compare scan and interval-halving work and include preparation in a repeated-query decision.
Explain what later correctness proofs and growth bounds must establish beyond a few successful runs.

blocks.title: Start here: the route through Algorithm Analysis
blocks.text: You need variables, integer comparisons, functions, loops, and indexed sequences. The examples use C++20, but the reasoning applies beyond C++. Read this unit in order: count search work; prove a loop correct; describe growth with bounds; build binary search; analyze insertion sort; explain merge sort. Logarithms, invariants, and recurrences are introduced before they are used in detail. The final lesson combines the techniques in a workload decision.

Suppose a library receives an integer book identifier and needs to answer whether that identifier is present in a collection. Before choosing a clever search, state the contract: accept a finite sequence of integer identifiers and one target; return true exactly when at least one sequence element equals the target; leave the sequence unchanged. An empty sequence is valid and must return false. This is a membership question. Returning a position, returning the first duplicate, or counting all duplicates would be different contracts.

The contract tells us what counts as a correct answer. Analysis asks a second question: which resources does a correct method require? Let n be the number of sequence elements. For now, one examination means choosing one element and comparing its value with the target. A scan uses one equality comparison per examination; a binary-search decision might use two different comparisons on the same element. We will not silently treat those as the same primitive-operation count. We are initially counting element examinations, not CPU instructions or seconds.

Our representation is an in-memory indexed sequence, with fixed-width integers and constant-cost indexed access in the chosen model. The vector is already available when a search begins. File loading, constructing the vector, displaying results, allocating storage, and preparing an ordering are outside this initial search count. This boundary makes the count useful and reproducible. It does not make the excluded work disappear from a complete application. Comparing long text, following linked nodes, or reading blocks from a disk requires a different account of costs.

A scan begins at index zero and moves one place right after each failed equality test. In [2, 6, 9, 13, 18, 25, 34, 47], searching for 25 examines six elements: the five earlier values rule out those positions, and the sixth supplies a match. Searching for 20 examines all eight before reporting absence. The input size is eight in both cases, yet the observed work differs. A statement about one execution therefore needs both the sequence and the target.

blocks.prompt: A collection contains [4, 11, 4]. If a search stops at the first 4, has it satisfied the membership contract? What changes if the requested output is the number of copies?
blocks.explanation: It satisfies membership because one equality is enough to establish existence. It has not established the number of copies: an unexamined position may contain another 4. A counting contract usually requires processing the remaining elements or using additional maintained information. The difference comes from the required answer, not a disagreement about how fast the same algorithm runs.

blocks.prompt: An empty sequence leads to zero element examinations. Does that establish zero running time?
blocks.explanation: No. The counted resource is only element examinations. Calling the function, checking that the loop cannot start, and returning a result still require work in a normal execution model. Zero examinations is the exact boundary-case count; constant total work is a separate description. Never infer a stopwatch reading from a counter that excludes most instructions.

parts.title: Trace and run the counted search

blocks.text: The following complete program exposes the scan counter. std::vector<int> stores the integer sequence; std::size_t is the unsigned size/index type used here. The const reference lets scan read the existing sequence without copying or modifying it. The reference named examinations is an output parameter: resetting it at the start makes each call report its own work. The increment is immediately before the equality test, so both a successful test and a failed test count once. In main, the range-for visits targets 25 and 20 in turn. std::boolalpha prints Boolean results as true or false. The {} argument constructs an empty vector for that call; the temporary remains alive while scan reads it.

blocks.caption: C++20 — count equality examinations on fixed small inputs; no program input is required

blocks.code:
25: found=true, examinations=6
20: found=false, examinations=8
empty: found=false, examinations=0
blocks.caption: Expected standard output

blocks.text: The loop condition is checked before values[i] is read. That is why the empty call is safe and why index values.size() is never examined. If a match occurs, the function returns immediately with the increment already recorded. If all tests fail, reaching the end means every allowed index was examined and none matched. Changing the target to 2 gives one examination; changing it to 47 gives eight. Use Edit and run to predict these counts before making the changes.

Now exploit a stronger input promise: the same eight values are already sorted. A binary membership search keeps an interval [low, high), including low and excluding high. Initially it is [0, 8). Choose mid = low + (high - low) / 2 using integer division. A too-small value rules out mid and all earlier candidates; a too-large value rules out mid and all later candidates. An equality answers membership. The trace below counts each chosen element once even if its decision uses more than one value comparison.

blocks.code:
Sorted identifiers: [2, 6, 9, 13, 18, 25, 34, 47]
Target 25:
[0,8): mid=4, value=18 -> low=5
[5,8): mid=6, value=34 -> high=6
[5,6): mid=5, value=25 -> found (3 examinations)

Target 20:
[0,8): mid=4, value=18 -> low=5
[5,8): mid=6, value=34 -> high=6
[5,6): mid=5, value=25 -> high=5
[5,5): empty -> absent (3 examinations)
blocks.caption: Original worked traces — counted element examinations, not timing measurements

blocks.text: After examining 18, sortedness tells us that every earlier value is also too small for either target. That implication justifies discarding five positions. After examining 34, only index five remains. The two traces share their first two steps but finish for different reasons: an observed equality versus an empty set of possible positions. Without sortedness, a large middle value says nothing reliable about values on its right. Halving an arbitrary array would be a faster way to obtain an unjustified answer.

blocks.prompt: Trace binary membership search for target 1 in the displayed sequence. How does this compare with the trace for 25?
blocks.explanation: The examined values are 18 at index 4, 9 at index 2, 6 at index 1, and 2 at index 0. Each is too large, so high becomes 4,2,1,0 in turn. The interval is then empty after four examinations. Target 25 took three. A logarithmic growth claim does not promise that every query on the same-sized sequence takes an identical number of steps.

blocks.prompt: The scan counter is moved after the equality test and executes only when the value did not match. What does the counter report for target 25, and why is that no longer our metric?
blocks.explanation: It reports five because the successful sixth examination returns before reaching the increment. The code now counts failed examinations rather than all examinations. Either metric can be defined, but mixing them makes comparisons misleading. Place instrumentation where it records precisely the event named in the analysis.

parts.title: Account for preparation and state the limits

blocks.text: To summarize many inputs, first specify the case. For the scan, among sequences and targets with n elements, an absent target requires n examinations; that is a worst case. For nonempty sequences, a target at the first position needs one; that is a best case. An average requires a stated distribution of inputs and targets. Neither the middle position nor half of the worst case automatically defines an average. The next modules will make these distinctions precise.

Repeated interval halving explains why binary search has logarithmic worst-case examinations under this indexed model. A scan has linear worst-case examinations. These are growth descriptions as n increases, not exact counts for every input. Big-O notation expresses an eventual upper bound up to a fixed multiplier; it is not an equality sign for work and it does not itself mean worst case. The growth-bounds lesson will derive the definitions and show how to select the relevant case function.

Preparation belongs in the final decision. Consider an explicitly hypothetical workload in common accounting units: preparing a sorted copy costs 60 units, one binary query costs 4, and one scan costs 8. For q independent membership queries on unchanged data, the strategies cost 60 + 4q and 8q. One query costs 64 versus 8. Twenty queries cost 140 versus 160. Preparing once helps in the second scenario but wastes work in the first. These invented coefficients illustrate how to combine costs; they are not measured performance or a bound for a particular sorting routine.

blocks.code:
Hypothetical unchanged-data workload
q queries       prepare + binary       repeated scans
1               60 + 4 = 64            8
15              60 + 60 = 120          120
20              60 + 80 = 140          160

60 + 4q < 8q
60 < 4q
q > 15
blocks.caption: Original accounting example — preparation included, all costs in the same invented unit

blocks.text: If the collection changes, the sorted representation must be maintained or rebuilt before its ordering can justify a later search. If preserving arrival order matters, sorting the original may violate a requirement, while a copy consumes additional memory. If the collection is linked rather than indexed, reaching a middle position may require many pointer traversals despite few value comparisons. These are reasons to name the representation, mutation pattern, required result, and memory budget alongside the growth bound.

blocks.prompt: With the displayed hypothetical costs, do exactly fifteen queries justify claiming that preparation saves work? What is the first integer query count that does?
blocks.explanation: At fifteen the two totals are equal:120 units. Equality is not a saving. The inequality reduces to q>15, so sixteen is the first integer count with a strict saving:60+64=124 versus 128. A different preparation cost or query distribution would move this crossover; the number is a result of this stated model only.

blocks.prompt: A benchmark finds that the eight-element scan finishes sooner than a binary search. Does that refute logarithmic search growth? What evidence would you collect next?
blocks.explanation: No. Small-input timings include constants, branching, call overhead, the implementation, and the measurement method. A growth statement describes a named resource over increasing input sizes under assumptions. Check that both implementations answer the same contract, count the stated events over several sizes and cases, include preparation, and use careful timing only for the actual deployment question. One small benchmark neither proves nor disproves an asymptotic claim.

blocks.text: You now have a reusable analysis checklist: define the answer, identify valid inputs, name the representation, choose a resource, trace contrasting cases, and include setup in the workload. You have also seen why counts alone cannot establish correctness. Continue to Prove a loop correct, where the scan becomes a vehicle for explaining why every permitted input is handled, including an empty sequence and repeated values. Later lessons replace informal growth descriptions with bounds and connect both techniques to sorting.
